title: The Paper Company That Became Dangote's Obajana Cement Works
dek: In 2002 Aliko Dangote, then Nigeria's leading cement importer, took over a state company that existed only on paper and set out to build the plant that would replace his own imports.

story.company: Dangote Group (Obajana Cement, later Dangote Cement)
story.event: Moving from importing cement to building the Obajana plant
story.summary: In 2002, as Nigeria's government began tying cement import licences to local production, Aliko Dangote's group, a major importer of bagged and bulk cement, took over Obajana Cement, a Kogi State company with no factory. The greenfield plant, estimated by the IFC at $798 million and financed with about 40% group equity and loans from Nigerian and international lenders, was commissioned in 2007 with 5 million tonnes a year of capacity. In 2022 the Kogi State government disputed the original transfer.
paragraphs: In 2002 Dangote Industries took over Obajana Cement from the government of Kogi State, which had registered the company a decade earlier. There was no factory. Aliko Dangote's group was then known as an importer. Founded in 1981 to trade bagged cement, rice, sugar and salt, it had moved on to shipping bulk cement into terminals at Apapa and Port Harcourt and bagging it for sale.

The country depended on imports. By the cement makers' association's count, Nigerian factories supplied about a quarter of the cement sold in 2002; Dangote later put imports at almost 90 per cent. That year Olusegun Obasanjo's government began granting import licences only to importers who could show they were building factories at home, and Dangote has said Obasanjo challenged him to cut the country's dependence. Trading was the easier life, but in his view "Trading does not add value and is just a temporary thing."

What he chose was large. Lenders in 2005 described a greenfield works in rural Kogi State with its own 135-megawatt gas power station, a 94-kilometre gas pipeline, a limestone quarry, a dam and housing for staff. The International Finance Corporation put the cost at $798 million: $319 million of the group's own equity, the rest loans from Nigerian and foreign lenders. The European Investment Bank expected the plant to replace about 60 per cent of cement imports, the trade Dangote's own terminals lived on.

The IFC's 2005 summary expected commissioning that year. The plant opened in 2007 with two lines and 5 million tonnes a year, then the largest cement works in sub-Saharan Africa. A third line followed in 2012, the year Nigeria issued no cement import licences. "Before I started manufacturing I do not have a single gray hair," Dangote said in 2021. The deal that began it is still contested: in 2022 the Kogi State government declared the transfer void, said it had no evidence of payment and shut the plant's gates. The company called this illegal.

quote.text: they who exercise it draw no man near to them except for their own interests; appearing as friends when it is to their own advantage, they stand not by a man in the hour of his need.
quote.thinker: Rabban Gamaliel, son of Rabbi Judah the Prince
quote.source_title: Pirke Avot: The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, tr. Joseph I. Gorfinkle, Project Gutenberg eBook #8547
quote.connection: Dangote judged trading the temporary business. Rabban Gamaliel, speaking of the ruling power, points to something else that does not last: the friendship of those who govern. Obajana grew from a federal policy and a state agreement, and twenty years later a state government tried to take it back.

reflection: Most serious work depends on someone with power over it: a regulator, a funder, a hospital board, a ministry that can change a rule. Dangote built on a policy, and the policy served him for years. It also meant the work could be challenged by people he did not control.

Rabban Gamaliel does not tell you to avoid such people; he tells you to be on your guard and not to mistake their interest for friendship. That is worth knowing calmly, before you need it, and it says nothing about your worth if the support someday cools.
invitation: Write down one person or office whose goodwill your current work depends on, and one small step that would leave the work a little less exposed if that goodwill changed.

sources.title: Our History
sources.supports: Dangote Industries founded by Aliko Dangote in 1981 as a trading business importing bagged cement, rice, sugar, flour and salt; later importing bulk cement into the Apapa and Port Harcourt terminals and bagging it; the 1990s decision to move from trading to manufacturing; Kogi State incorporating Obajana Cement Plc in November 1992; acquisition from Kogi State in 2002 when no factory existed; construction begun in 2004; commissioning in 2007 with two lines and 5 Mta, the largest plant in sub-Saharan Africa; Line 3 in June 2012.

sources.title: Nigeria Operations
sources.supports: Obajana commissioned in 2007 with two lines totalling 5 Mta, then the largest cement factory in sub-Saharan Africa; extended to 10.25 Mta in 2012 with Line 3.

sources.title: Obajana Cement PLC (project 23237), Environmental Review Summary
sources.publisher: International Finance Corporation disclosure portal (approved May 2005)
sources.supports: Greenfield cement plant at Obajana, Kogi State, with a 135 MW captive gas power plant, a 94 km gas pipeline, a limestone quarry and conveyor, a dam and reservoir and a 328-unit staff housing complex; estimated cost of $798 million, financed by $319 million of sponsor equity (40%) and $479 million of long-term debt from local and international lenders; sponsor Dangote Industries; implementation started in 2003 with commissioning then expected in 2005.

sources.title: Obajana Cement Plant (project 20030482)
sources.supports: EIB finance of up to USD 150 million (EUR 123 million) for Obajana Cement PLC, a subsidiary of Dangote Industries; project cost of the order of USD 800 million; a new greenfield plant rated at 4.4 million tonnes a year for the national market; expected to substitute about 60% of current cement imports and save Nigeria over USD 500 million a year in hard currency.

sources.title: CMAN demands implementation of 2002 backward integration policy for cement (July 2009)
sources.supports: The 2002 backward integration policy requiring that cement import licences go only to importers who show proof of building local factories; locally made cement rising from 25.5% (2.07 million tonnes) of supply in 2002 to 47% in 2008; Nigeria's two largest importers also being local manufacturers; Dangote's petition to the President to ban cement imports.

sources.title: Nigeria: Changes for the cement industry (2013)
sources.supports: The Backward Integration Policy initially granting cement import licences only to companies signalling intent to build local capacity; capacity rising from 2 million tonnes in 2002 to 28 million tonnes by the end of 2012; no cement import licences issued in 2012.

sources.title: Dangote: Why I dumped trading for manufacturing (9 September 2021)
sources.publisher: ThisDay (Dike Onwuamaeze), from a conversation with Doyin Salami at the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria's 50th anniversary roundtable
sources.supports: 'Before I started manufacturing I do not have a single gray hair'; 'Trading does not add value and is just a temporary thing'; Dangote's statement that Nigeria was at one time importing almost 90 per cent of the cement it consumed; the decision to make Nigeria self-sufficient in cement and invest heavily in technology.

sources.title: Why it seems like we have a monopoly in refining, cement – Dangote (18 September 2025)
sources.supports: Dangote recalling that his entry into cement manufacturing was inspired by Olusegun Obasanjo, who challenged him to reduce Nigeria's dependence on imported cement, and that he built the Obajana plant in Kogi State.

sources.title: Kogi State insists no evidence of consideration paid by Dangote Industries Limited for transfer of Obajana Cement (8 October 2022)
sources.supports: The Kogi State government's 2022 position that the 2002 agreement and 2003 supplemental agreement transferring Obajana Cement were void and that there was no evidence of payment; the state shutting the plant's gates on 5 October 2022; Dangote Cement describing the shutdown as illegal.

sources.title: The man who built Nigeria (30 July 2025)
sources.supports: Dangote Industries founded in 1981 as an importer of bagged cement and other commodities; Benue Cement stake bought in 2000; Obajana Cement bought in 2002, with its first line running by 2007; the 2022 court dispute with Kogi State over ownership.

cross_checks.claim: Dangote Industries began in 1981 as an importer of bagged cement and other commodities.
In 2002 the group took over Obajana Cement from Kogi State, when no factory existed.
From 2002 the government granted cement import licences only to importers building local factories.
The Obajana project was estimated to cost about $800 million, financed by group equity and loans that included the IFC and EIB.
Obajana was commissioned in 2007 with two lines and 5 million tonnes a year.
In 2022 the Kogi State government disputed the transfer of Obajana.

research_notes: Import dependence: Dangote said in 2021 that Nigeria was at one time importing 'almost 90 per cent' of its cement; the Cement Manufacturers Association (Vanguard, 2009) put locally made cement at 25.5% of supply in 2002, implying roughly three-quarters imported. The story gives both with attribution. Cost: the IFC's 2005 summary gives $798 million and the EIB 'of the order of USD 800 million'; a CemNet report seen only in search snippets gave $1.2 billion for lines 1 and 2, and CemNet's pages sit behind a bot challenge, so that figure is not used. Capacity: the 2005 lender documents describe 4.4 million tonnes a year; the company says it was commissioned at 5 million tonnes a year with two lines; the story uses the company figure for the plant as opened. Dates: the IFC says implementation began in 2003 with commissioning expected in 2005; the company says construction began in 2004 and commissioning was in 2007; Oxford Business Group's 2013 company profile says 2003, which conflicts with every other source and is not used. The story gives 2007 and notes the earlier expectation. 'First venture': the IFC calls Obajana the sponsor's first venture into cement production, but the group had bought a controlling stake in the producing Benue Cement Company in 2000 (company history, Global Cement); the story avoids the word 'first'. The Kogi State government's 2002 agreement date (30 July 2002) and its claim of no payment come from a state committee report quoted by Nairametrics; Global Cement reports that the state took the company to court; the story gives the state's claims as claims and the company's response, without judging them. Dangote's quotations come from a 2021 roundtable reported by ThisDay; 'gray hair' and the tense ('I do not have') are as printed. Obasanjo's challenge is Dangote's own 2025 recollection as reported by Nigerian NewsDirect. Funding is 'mixed': 40% sponsor equity and 60% debt from local banks and development lenders including the IFC and EIB.
